name: Re-authenticating
explanation: Say a user's login session expires while they're in the middle of something. Logging back in should let them pick up exactly where they left off, without losing whatever they had entered or in progress. This means the underlying system needs to preserve draft data, like an in-progress form or shopping cart. That data must survive the re-authentication step instead of being discarded the moment the session times out.
whoItAffects: Some people take longer to complete tasks. This can be due to a cognitive disability, a motor disability, or reliance on assistive technology that needs more time and steps. These same people are more likely to have a session expire mid-task in the first place. Losing everything they've entered, after already investing real time and effort, punishes exactly the users who needed more time to begin with. Without this protection, a session timeout can turn a minor delay into redoing an entire form or checkout from scratch.
howToTest: Start filling out a multi-step form or a lengthy input. Then deliberately wait for the session to expire, or force a logout if you can. Log back in and check whether your in-progress data is still there, or whether you're forced to start over from a blank form. If any meaningful progress is lost purely because of the re-authentication step, this fails.

check.question: A user is halfway through a long multi-page insurance application when their session times out. After logging back in, all previously entered fields are gone and they must start the entire application over. Does this pass SC 2.2.5 Re-authenticating?
choices: Yes, because session timeouts are a standard security practice
No, because the user's in-progress data was lost instead of preserved across re-authentication
Yes, because the user was warned about the timeout in advance
It depends only on how long the original session lasted
